note.note:
Consult Summary:
- 19-year-old female with 3 days of dysuria and lower abdominal cramping; reported a small amount of visible haematuria earlier today and malodorous urine.
- Clinical impression: probable uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection (UTI). Planned short-course oral antibiotic (nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim) and conservative measures; return if symptoms worsen or fail to improve.

Problem List:

Issue 1: Suspected uncomplicated urinary tract infection (dysuria, haematuria)
- Presentation: 3 days of burning/stinging pain with urination and intermittent lower abdominal crampy pain; patient reports a small amount of visible blood in urine earlier today and an unusual urine odor.
- Systems review: No increased urinary frequency reported; no nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, flank pain, or back pain.
- Social/sexual history relevant: Sexually active with a single boyfriend for ~2 months; uses condoms. No prior STD screening reported.
- Medications/trial therapies: Patient tried over-the-counter bicarbonate a few days ago without improvement.
- Examination: Doctor intended to examine but no examination findings documented in transcript.
- Differential/assessment: Clinician assessment = likely simple UTI (bladder infection).
- Management: Plan to prescribe either nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim as a three-day course (one tablet twice daily for three days; strength and route not documented). Advice to increase fluid intake, consider cranberry juice, avoid sexual intercourse while symptomatic if possible, and continue barrier contraception. Advised to return or call if no improvement by end of the week or sooner if developing fever, back pain, or worsening systemic symptoms (concern for ascending infection/pyelonephritis).
- Additional recommendation: Clinician suggested pregnancy test if there is any concern about possible pregnancy.

Issue 2: Allergy — Clindamycin
- Reaction: Patient reports allergy to clindamycin causing swelling.
- Implication: Avoid clindamycin; clinician aware when selecting antibiotics.

Issue 3: Past functional bowel disorder (irritable bowel syndrome)
- History: Patient reports past history of IBS.
- Current status: No active diarrhoea or bowel symptoms at time of consult.

Medications:
- Planned antibiotic: Nitrofurantoin OR Trimethoprim — prescribed as "one tablet twice a day for three days"; medication name selected but strength and route not documented.
- Over-the-counter bicarbonate taken a few days ago for symptom relief (no benefit).
- No regular prescription medications reported.

Allergies:
- Clindamycin — swelling reaction.

Past Medical History:
- Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).
- No other chronic medical problems reported.

Social History:
- Lives in a flat with friends near college.
- Student studying biology.
- Sexually active with one boyfriend; uses condoms.
- Non-smoker.
- Alcohol: social drinking on weekends.

Preventative History:
- Has never had an STD screen (patient reports no prior testing).
- Last menstrual period approximately 2–3 weeks ago.
- No other preventative care (cervical screening, mammogram, PSA, FOBT, bone density, vaccinations, recent optometry or skin check) documented.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not documented.
- Examination findings: No physical exam documented; doctor stated they would proceed to exam but no findings recorded.

Plan:
- Prescribe short-course antibiotic for presumed uncomplicated UTI (nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim; one tablet twice daily for three days — strength/route not documented).
- Advise increased fluid intake and consider cranberry juice.
- Recommend avoiding sexual activity while symptomatic if possible; continue barrier contraception.
- If symptoms persist by end of the week or if fever, flank/back pain, or systemic illness develop, return or call urgently for reassessment (possible progression to pyelonephritis).
- Consider pregnancy test if patient is concerned.
- Consider STI screening given sexual activity and no prior testing (not explicitly ordered in transcript; clinician discussed history only).

document_quality:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs, physical examination findings, urine dipstick/urinalysis results, urine culture results, exact antibiotic choice (nitrofurantoin vs trimethoprim) with medication strength and confirmed route, pregnancy test result, and explicit STI screening/testing orders.
- Internal conflicts: brief verbal uncertainty about fever early in the consult ("think so") followed by patient clarification of no fever — conflict noted and later resolved by patient stating no fever.
- Transcript quality: audio mostly clear with intermittent brief interruptions; overall adequate for clinical documentation.
